title: Morning fog and afternoon puffs
teaches: Will the morning grey burn off, and are those white puffs harmless? What a cloud is, how a still night makes fog and stratus, and how rising air builds fair-weather cumulus

parts.title: What a cloud is made of

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: A cloud is liquid water droplets (or ice), not water vapour.
Water vapour condenses into droplets when air cools to a certain temperature, its **dew point**. The more vapour in the air, the higher its dew point, and the muggier it feels.

A clear, calm, damp night chills the air lying on the ground until it reaches its dew point: **fog**. Lifted off the ground, the same layer is **stratus**. The morning sun clears it from the bottom up.

Rising air expands and cools, about 10 °C per kilometre (5.4 °F per 1,000 feet). Cumulus bases sit about 125 m up for every °C between the temperature and the dew point at the ground (about 220 feet per °F).
Sun-warmed ground sends up bubbles of air that turn into flat-bottomed heaps: **cumulus**. Small heaps that stay small are fair weather, and they fade at sunset.

blocks.text: Two skies greet most summer mornings. At dawn a grey blanket hides the hills or fills the valley; by noon it has gone, and white puffs with flat bottoms are drifting over the fields. Will the grey burn off in time? Are the puffs harmless? This lesson answers both, starting with what any cloud is made of.

Think of a boiling kettle. The white plume over the spout is not water vapour. Water vapour is water as a gas, made of individual molecules flying about on their own among the nitrogen and oxygen molecules of the air, and it is completely invisible. If you look closely at a boiling kettle, there is a clear gap right at the spout where the steam is still vapour. The white plume begins a finger’s width further out, where the vapour cools and its molecules clump together into microscopic liquid droplets. Individual gas molecules let light pass straight through, whereas liquid droplets are large enough to scatter light in every direction. Billions of droplets scattering sunlight in all directions look white.

A cloud is the same thing on a much larger scale. It is not water vapour, but tiny droplets of liquid water (or, very high up, tiny ice crystals) suspended in the air. So asking “why is there a cloud here?” is really asking “why did invisible vapour condense into liquid droplets here, and not over there?”

Why does vapour turn to liquid at all? Water molecules are slightly sticky, and now and then a few that bump together cling. In warm air they jiggle so fast that they soon shake free again; in colder air they move more slowly and stay stuck more often. And the more water molecules crowd into each cubic metre, the more often they meet. So at any temperature there is a limit to how crowded vapour can be before molecules stick faster than they shake apart, and past that limit the excess condenses into droplets. Warm air has a high limit: a cubic metre at 30 °C can keep about 30 grams of water as vapour, roughly two spoonfuls. At 0 °C the limit drops below 5 grams.

Now take some air with a fixed amount of water vapour in it and cool it down. At first nothing visible happens, because the vapour has not reached its limit yet. Keep cooling the air, and that limit shrinks until it equals the amount of water vapour actually present. That temperature is the air’s **dew point**. Cool the air below its dew point and the excess vapour condenses into droplets. It takes its name from morning dew on grass, where the cold blades chill the thin layer of air touching them below its dew point.

blocks.caption: A sealed jar of air with some water vapour in it. The violet curve is how much vapour there is room for at each temperature.
blocks.task: Cool the jar until it fogs.

blocks.text: Move the water slider in the jar and notice how the dew point behaves. First, the dew point depends only on how crowded the vapour is (how many grams of water vapour are in each cubic metre), not on how warm the air happens to be right now. (It is a temperature, but it is the temperature the air *would* have to be cooled to; warming or cooling the air does not move it.) If you add water vapour, the dew point goes up because the molecules are more crowded and need less cooling before they start sticking together. That makes the dew point a direct measure of how humid the air is. You can feel it on your skin. With the dew point below about 10 °C (50 °F) the air feels crisp and dry; around 16 to 18 °C (60 to 65 °F) it turns sticky; above 20 °C (68 °F) it feels muggy and oppressive, because sweat can barely evaporate.
Second, you don’t have to add any water to air to make a cloud. You only have to cool the air down to its dew point.

In the atmosphere, water vapour needs a surface to condense onto. A cluster of just a few water molecules is so tiny and tightly curved that molecules escape from its surface far more easily than new ones stick, so it breaks apart before it can grow. Specks of dust, smoke, or sea salt give water molecules a larger surface to gather on, and every lungful of outdoor air contains millions of such specks. The resulting cloud droplets are tiny, about a hundredth of a millimetre across. Because of air resistance, droplets that small fall at less than a centimetre per second, slow enough for the slightest upward breeze to keep them aloft.

blocks.caption: Where a droplet can start, and how small it is.

blocks.text: So making a cloud comes down to one question: what cools the air to its dew point? The sky has two main ways. It can chill air right where it sits, by cooling the ground underneath it, or it can lift the air up high, where air cools all by itself. The morning grey is the first way; the afternoon puffs are the second. This lesson takes them in that order, starting with **fog**.
To make fog, a broad layer of air has to be cooled gently all together, without lifting it at all. The night does exactly that.

After sunset the ground keeps radiating its heat away as infrared light, which our eyes cannot see, and under a clear sky that heat escapes straight out to space. Soil, stubble and grass radiate strongly; clear air, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, hardly radiates at all. So the ground cools much faster than the air above it. By dawn on a still, clear night the grass can be several degrees colder than the air at head height, which is why you can find frost on a car roof while a thermometer at eye level still reads above freezing.

The chilled ground cools the air resting on it, the way your hand cools on a cold windowpane, and gentle stirring spreads that chill up through the lowest few tens of metres. A cloud overhead spoils it all: its droplets send the ground’s heat back down like a blanket, which is why a cloudy night stays mild while a clear one turns cold.

Cold air does the opposite. It is denser than the air around it, so it sinks and spreads along the ground. On a still night you can feel it as you walk downhill: the chilled air slides off the slopes and pools in the hollows and valley bottoms, which is why fog so often fills the low places first.

Cooling from below leaves the coldest, densest air at the bottom with warmer air above it. Normally the air gets colder as you go up, so this arrangement is upside down, and it is called an **inversion**. It is the most stable arrangement there is: the heaviest air is already as low as it can go, so nothing bubbles up through it. You can often see one on a still morning, when chimney smoke rises a little way and then spreads out flat.

Notice what is not happening to this chilled air: it is not going anywhere. The same grams of water vapour sit in each cubic metre all night, so its dew point stays where it was while its temperature drops toward it, just as in the jar.

blocks.caption: A night in a valley.
blocks.task: Find a night that ends in fog by dawn.

blocks.text: A cloud that forms on the ground is **fog**. In the figure, the cooling slows down later in the night because colder ground radiates less heat. Watch what the wind slider does as well. A light breeze stirs only the bottom few dozen metres of chilled air, spreading the cold upward so the fog grows deeper. A strong wind stirs a much deeper layer, mixing warmer air down from above the inversion so the air near the ground never gets cold enough for fog to form.

Fog and **stratus** are the exact same cloud; the name only indicates whether the cloud base touches the ground. When a morning breeze or the first warmth of the sun evaporates the bottom of a fog bank, the layer left hanging above is stratus: a flat, uniform sheet with no distinct features, often low enough to hide the hilltops. Stratus also forms during the day or night whenever warm, moist air drifts across cold ground or cold sea water and gets chilled from below. In either case, stable air is cooled gently as a wide layer, forming an unbroken sheet.

blocks.caption: The same layer of cloud, seen from the valley floor.

blocks.text: Seen from below, stratus looks grey. It is made of the same water droplets as a white cumulus cloud, but because a stratus layer covers the sky, you see only its shaded underside while its sunlit top faces away from you. The flat base of a cumulus cloud looks grey for the same reason; a cumulus looks bright white only where you can see sunlight hitting its sides and rounded top. If you fly above a stratus deck, its upper surface is dazzling white.

A thick layer of stratus can bring drizzle. The tiny droplets inside bump into one another as they drift, and now and then two merge. After an hour or so in a thick layer, enough merging takes place to produce drops a few tenths of a millimetre across. Those larger drops fall at one or two metres per second, far faster than any gentle air current in a quiet, stable layer can hold up, so they sink out of the cloud as drizzle.

Stratus is more of a nuisance than a danger. It brings drizzle at worst, and it usually burns off by late morning. Sunlight filters through the layer and warms the ground, the ground warms the air from below, and once the air’s temperature climbs back above its dew point, the droplets evaporate back into vapour.

blocks.caption: A fog bank on a summer morning, from dawn to late morning.

blocks.text: So the morning grey has a timetable. After a clear, calm, damp night, expect fog or low stratus at dawn, thinning from below as the sun climbs and usually gone by mid to late morning. A grey layer that came in on a wind, or sits under a thick cloud above it, can hang on much longer.

By late morning, though, after the fog has gone, a different cloud usually appears: white heaps a kilometre or more above the fields, far from any cold ground. Something else is cooling that air. It is being lifted.
To see why lifting cools air, follow a single blob of air on its way up. In meteorology, a blob like this is called a **parcel**.

Of course, a parcel has no skin around it, and at its edges it is always mixing with the surrounding air. Even so, air genuinely moves in distinct blobs. A bubble of warm air rising off a sunny field can be a few hundred metres across and hold together for many minutes; hawks and glider pilots find these bubbles and circle inside them to climb. Because a blob that size mixes only around its outer edges, its core carries its own temperature and moisture upward. Treating a rising bubble as a self-contained parcel is a simplification, like a physicist’s frictionless ball, but it captures the essential physics.

Air near the ground is compressed by the weight of all the air piled above it, which comes to about ten tonnes on every square metre. We don’t feel crushed because the air and fluids inside our bodies push outward just as hard as the atmosphere pushes in. If you climb one kilometre, you leave about a tenth of the atmosphere below you, so there is a tenth less weight on top and the surrounding pressure is a tenth weaker.

When a parcel of air rises into that lower pressure, the air inside it is still at the higher pressure it had lower down, pushing outward harder than the air around it pushes in, so the parcel expands until its internal pressure drops to match the air outside.

When air expands, it cools. You have probably felt the opposite effect when pumping up a bicycle tyre, where compressing the air makes the pump warm. You can see expansion cooling directly if you pop open a bottle of fizzy drink: as the pressure drops, the gas in the neck expands, cools past its dew point, and forms a brief wisp of fog.

Temperature is simply a measure of how fast molecules are jostling around. As a rising parcel expands, its molecules spend energy pushing the surrounding air out of the way, so they come away moving a little more slowly. Nothing cold has touched the parcel; it cools because its own molecules did the work of expanding.

blocks.caption: A parcel of air rising from the ground. Nothing is added or taken away: the same molecules just spread out.

blocks.text: As long as no cloud has formed yet, a rising parcel cools at a steady rate of about 10 °C for every kilometre it climbs (9.8 °C, to be exact, or about 5.4 °F for every 1,000 feet). This rate isn’t a rough average across different days. It follows directly from how hard gravity pulls on the atmosphere and how much heat energy air stores, so it is the same every day.

The parcel’s dew point also drops as it climbs, but much more slowly, at about 2 °C per kilometre. The parcel hasn’t lost any water, yet as it expands, the same water vapour is spread across a larger volume, leaving fewer grams of vapour in each cubic metre. Less crowded vapour has a lower dew point, just like sliding the water control down a little in the jar figure.

In a [[rising parcel|parcel]], two temperatures are converging: its actual temperature falls by about 10 °C per kilometre, while its [[dew point|dew]] falls by about 2 °C per kilometre. The gap between them closes by about 8 °C for every kilometre the parcel climbs.

blocks.caption: A parcel of air at ground level, 24 °C with a dew point of 12 °C.
blocks.task: Lift the air until it turns to cloud.

blocks.text: Where the two lines meet, the parcel has cooled to its dew point. Its vapour condenses into droplets, and the parcel becomes cloud. That height is the **cloud base**, and you can work it out directly from the ground readings. Because the gap closes by 8 °C every kilometre, each degree of gap at the ground takes about 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 metres of lift to close. At the ground this morning, the gap is 24 − 12 = 12 °C, which puts the cloud base at about 12 × 125 = 1,500 metres above the ground. In feet the rule is about 220 feet for every °F of gap, or 1,000 feet for every 4.4 °F.

You can see this relationship all summer. On a muggy day, the dew point starts out close to the air temperature, so rising air reaches condensation quickly and clouds form low. On a dry day, the gap is wide and cloud bases sit high. Try moving the dew point slider to see how the cloud base shifts.

Sunlight passes through clear air almost without warming it. The ground absorbs the sunlight instead, and the warm ground heats the air touching it. Different surfaces warm up at different rates: dark rock, bare fields, and roofs get hot quickly, while a lake or a damp forest spends much of the sun’s energy evaporating water and stays cooler.

Over a hot patch of ground, the air warms, becomes less dense than the cooler air around it, and eventually breaks free to rise as a bubble called a **thermal**. A thermal behaves just like the parcel we followed earlier, cooling at 10 °C per kilometre as it expands and closing the gap to its dew point. Where temperature and dew point meet, water vapour condenses into droplets and from there up the thermal becomes visible as a heap of cloud: a **cumulus**.

blocks.caption: A sunny morning over farm country. Thermals rise from the warmest ground.
blocks.task: Bring the sun up until two clouds have formed.

blocks.text: In the figure, notice that every heap starts at the same height, giving cumulus clouds **flat bases** all at one level. You might expect a bubble rising off the hottest rock to start out much warmer and reach its dew point much higher up. In practice, by mid-morning the rising thermals have stirred the lowest kilometre of the sky so thoroughly that the air across the valley has nearly uniform temperature and moisture. A bubble breaks away as soon as it is a degree or so warmer than its surroundings, which changes its condensation height by only a hundred metres or so. Seen from across the valley, the cloud bases line up along a flat level.

Moving the **moisture** slider shifts that level up or down. Humid air starts with a small gap between temperature and dew point, so its cloud bases are low; dry air starts with a wide gap, so its bases are high. Because a thermal only keeps rising while it remains warmer than the air around it, on very dry days the rising bubbles lose their temperature lead and stop climbing before they ever reach their dew point. The thermals then stay completely invisible, leaving a blue, cloudless sky that is still bumpy for gliders.

Between the cumulus clouds, the sky stays clear. Every bit of air that rises in a thermal must be replaced by air sinking somewhere else. As the air between the thermals sinks into higher pressure, it is compressed and warms by 10 °C per kilometre, moving its temperature further above its dew point so no cloud can form.

blocks.caption: A fair-weather cumulus, and the air moving around it.

blocks.text: Small cumulus scattered across a blue sky are the best weather there is, and they are called fair-weather cumulus. They appear with the morning sun and fade around sunset, when the ground stops heating the air and the thermals shut down.

How tall a heap grows depends on the air above it, and the next lessons take that up. A warm layer a little way up can stop the heaps and flatten them into a grey sheet (Lesson 2); air that keeps getting colder fast with height can let them tower into thunderstorms (Lesson 5). For now, the rule of the hay field: small, flat-bottomed heaps that stay small all day are fair weather.

So the two skies of a summer morning are the sky’s two basic textures. Stratus is air chilled where it lies, in a still layer; cumulus is air lifted in bubbles. Every other cloud in this workbook is one of those two ideas, or a mix of them, at one of three heights.
The drawings in this lesson are clean; real skies are not. Here are this lesson’s two clouds in photographs, side by side, and the one thing that tells them apart. Keep it in mind for the check.

options.tell: Look for edges. Stratus has none: one grey lid with no shape of its own, often hiding the hilltops. Each cumulus heap has an outline, a flat base and a bright, bulging top.

blocks.text: The photos below are real skies. Name each one: cumulus heaps or a stratus blanket.
**Cumulus**: separate heaps with flat bases, bright tops, and blue sky between them. **Stratus**: a flat, uniform grey layer with no gaps, often hiding the hills.

blocks.caption: The sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: A grey layer has covered the sky all evening, and a brisk wind is blowing. Will there be fog in the valley by dawn?
options: Yes: a grey evening like this one always settles into fog by dawn
Unlikely: the cloud keeps the ground warm and the wind mixes the chill away
Yes, but only if the wind picks up and pushes the cloud down to the ground
items.why: Fog needs the ground to lose its heat to a clear sky, and calm or nearly calm air so the chill stays at the bottom. A cloud layer sends heat back down like a blanket, and a brisk wind mixes warmer air down from above.

items.question: At 7 a.m. the valley is full of fog. By 9 a.m. you can see across the fields, but a flat grey ceiling still hides the hilltops. What happened?
options: The sun warmed the ground, which cleared the fog from the bottom up, leaving stratus
A second, higher cloud blew in from the hills and settled over the old fog
The fog floated up off the fields because cloud is lighter than the air
items.why: Fog clears from the bottom up: the sun warms the ground, the ground warms the air touching it, and the lowest droplets evaporate first. The layer left hanging above is the same cloud, now called stratus, and it usually goes next.

items.question: After a clear, still, damp night, a grey blanket lies on the ground at dawn and hides the hilltops. When can a plane expect to take off?
options: Right away: fog is at its thinnest at dawn, before the sun stirs it up
Not today: a blanket this thick at dawn means a storm is close behind
Mid to late morning, once the sun has warmed the ground and burned it off
items.why: On a clear, still night the ground cools the air above it below its dew point. After sunrise the sun warms the ground, the ground warms the air, and once the air is warmer than its dew point again the fog evaporates, usually by mid to late morning.

items.question: On a muggy morning the temperature is 24 °C (75 °F) and the dew point 20 °C (68 °F). Will the cumulus bases be low or high today?
options: High: about 2,500 metres up, because warm air rises a long way
Low: about 500 metres up, because the gap is only 4 °C
None at all: air this warm is too warm to turn into cloud
items.why: A gap of 4 °C between temperature and dew point closes after about 4 × 125 = 500 metres of lift (in feet, a 7 °F gap at 220 feet a degree is about 1,500 feet), so humid air makes low bases.

items.question: Small, flat-bottomed heaps popped up mid-morning and have stayed small all day, drifting across a blue sky. Is it safe to leave cut hay out to dry?
options: Yes: fair-weather cumulus that stay small, and they will fade by evening
No: heaps that come back every morning are building up to rain by evening
Only if the wind drops, because wind is what turns small heaps into rain
items.why: Small cumulus that stay small are thermals that run into stable air a little above their bases, so they cannot grow tall. They come with the morning sun and fade when the ground stops heating the air: fair weather.

learned: A cloud is made of liquid droplets (or ice crystals), not water vapour. Air forms a cloud when it cools to its dew point, and the more water vapour a cubic metre of air contains, the higher its dew point: under 10 °C (50 °F) feels crisp, over 20 °C (68 °F) muggy.
Droplets need a speck of dust, smoke or salt to form on, and every lungful of air holds millions of them.

On a clear, calm night the ground radiates its heat to space and chills the air resting on it. Cold air stays at the bottom under warmer air, an inversion. When that still layer reaches its dew point it becomes fog; lifted off the ground it is stratus, which burns off from the bottom up by mid to late morning.
Rising air expands and cools by about 10 °C per kilometre (5.4 °F per 1,000 feet), while its dew point falls by about 2, so the gap closes by 8 °C per kilometre.
The cloud base sits about 125 m up for each °C between the temperature and dew point at the ground (about 220 feet per °F): low on humid days, high on dry ones.
Sun-warmed ground launches thermals that turn into flat-bottomed cumulus. Small heaps that stay small are fair weather, and fade at sunset.

what-is-a-cloud.title: What a cloud is
what-is-a-cloud.text: A cloud consists of tiny liquid droplets (or ice crystals), not water vapour. Air turns to cloud when cooled to its dew point, the temperature below which excess water vapour condenses into liquid; the more humid the air, the higher its dew point. Each droplet starts on a speck of dust, smoke or salt, and is about a hundredth of a millimetre across.

fog.title: Fog
fog.text: A cloud with its base on the ground. On a clear, still, damp night the ground radiates its heat to space faster than the air does, grows colder than the air, and chills the air resting on it to its dew point. The cold air stays at the bottom under warmer air (an inversion), so fog fills the low places first. A cloudy sky or a breeze prevents it. The morning sun clears it from the bottom up.

stratus.title: Stratus
stratus.text: A flat, uniform grey layer low enough to hide the hills, essentially fog whose base is off the ground. It forms by gentle cooling of stable air, either overnight or while drifting over cold ground or water. It brings light drizzle at most and often burns off by midday.

rising-air.title: Rising air
rising-air.text: Rising air expands into the lower pressure aloft and cools by about 10 °C per kilometre (5.4 °F per 1,000 feet) while its dew point falls by about 2 °C per kilometre, so the gap between them closes by 8 °C per kilometre. The cloud base forms about 125 m up for each °C between the temperature and dew point at the ground (about 220 feet per °F): low on humid days, high on dry ones.

cumulus.title: Cumulus
cumulus.text: Separate heaps of cloud with flat bases and bright, rounded tops, built by rising thermals on sunny days. Small ones indicate fair weather, while towers still growing tall at midday can bring afternoon showers.
